lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write $C=\sum_k c_k(X,Y)Z^k$. By the definition of $e$, every positive supported exponent $k$ is divisible by $s$, and some supported $k$ has $k/s
e0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. Lucas's theorem gives $ inom{k}{r}=0$ in $\mathbb F_p$ whenever $0<r<s$, while $ inom{k}{s}=k/s
e0$ for at least one supported exponent of minimal $p$-adic valuation. Hence all lower positive Hasse derivatives vanish and $\partial_Z^{[s]}C
e0$.

The polynomial $\partial_Z^{[s]}C$ has strictly smaller $Z$-degree than the irreducible polynomial $C$, so $\gcd(C,\partial_Z^{[s]}C)=1$. Moreover, $C\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z^s]$. Since $C$ is $Z$-dependent, one of its monomials has $Z$-exponent at least $s$, and therefore $\operatorname{wdeg}C\ge ds$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Assign weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Let $C=\sum_{k\ge0}c_k(X,Y)Z^k\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be irreducible and $Z$-dependent, and define

$$e:=\min\{v_p(k):k>0,\ c_k\ne0\},\qquad s:=p^e.$$

For the Hasse derivatives determined by

$$C(X,Y,Z+T)=\sum_{r\ge0}\partial_Z^{[r]}C(X,Y,Z)T^r,$$

one has $\partial_Z^{[r]}C=0$ for every $0<r<s$, while $\partial_Z^{[s]}C\ne0$, $\gcd(C,\partial_Z^{[s]}C)=1$, and $\operatorname{wdeg}C\ge ds$.
lemmas.title: Hasse Height

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For each $i$, the definition of the height gives $C_i=E_i(X,Y,Z^{s_i})$ for some polynomial $E_i$. The graph identity implies that $W=q(t)^{s_i}$ is a root of $E_i(L(t),W)$ in $\mathbb F_p[t][W]$. Hence

$$W-q(t)^{s_i}\mid E_i(L(t),W).$$

Substituting $W=Z^{s_i}$ and using Frobenius gives

$$Z^{s_i}-q(t)^{s_i}=(Z-q(t))^{s_i}\mid C_i(L(t),Z),$$

which proves the multiplicity assertion.

The ordinary product rule gives

$$B_Z\equiv c\,C_{i,Z}\prod_{j\ne i}C_j\pmod{C_i}.$$

Because the factors are distinct and irreducible, the product over $j\ne i$ is nonzero modulo $C_i$. Thus $C_i\mid B_Z$ exactly when $C_{i,Z}=0$. By the height conclusion from [P1], this occurs exactly when $s_i>1$. Since $B$ is squarefree, its greatest common divisor with $B_Z$ therefore has precisely the asserted factors.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $B=c\prod_{i=1}^r C_i\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$, where $c\in\mathbb F_p^\times$ and the $C_i$ are distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent polynomials with Hasse heights $s_i$. If an affine-line parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $q(t)\in\mathbb F_p[t]$ satisfy

$$C_i(L(t),q(t))\equiv0,$$

then

$$(Z-q(t))^{s_i}\mid C_i(L(t),Z)$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t,Z]$. Moreover, $\gcd(B,B_Z)$ has exactly the irreducible factors $C_i$ for which $s_i>1$.
lemmas.title: Vertical Multiplicity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Assume first that both $Z$-degrees are positive. Since $U$ and $V$ are coprime, their Sylvester resultant $R(X,Y)=\operatorname{Res}_Z(U,V)$ is nonzero. Every determinant term contains $s$ coefficients of $U$ and $r$ coefficients of $V$. Weighted homogeneity therefore bounds its ordinary degree in $X,Y$ by

$$\deg R\le su+rv-drs.$$

The further inequality follows from

$$(u-dr)(v-ds)\ge0,$$

which is equivalent to $su+rv-drs\le uv/d$.

For every $L\in\mathcal T$, specialization of the Sylvester determinant gives $R(L(t))\equiv0$, because the two specialized polynomials have the common root $q_L(t)$. Thus the affine linear equation defining $L$ divides $R$. Distinct underlying lines give distinct linear factors, and a nonzero bivariate polynomial has no more distinct affine-line factors than its total degree. If one $Z$-degree is zero, the same conclusion follows directly by counting the affine-line factors of the corresponding polynomial in $X,Y$. No leading coefficient is divided out.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $U,V\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ be nonzero and coprime, with

$$u=\operatorname{wdeg}U,\quad v=\operatorname{wdeg}V,\quad r=\deg_ZU,\quad s=\deg_ZV,$$

under the weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a set of distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_p^2$, each equipped with one polynomial $q_L$ of degree at most $d$, such that

$$U(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv V(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. Then

$$|\mathcal T|\le su+rv-drs\le\frac{uv}{d}.$$
lemmas.title: Weighted Resultants

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The Hasse product rule and the vanishing of all positive derivatives below order $s$ give

$$\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s=\sum_{i:s_i=s}\left(\partial_Z^{[s]}C_i\right)\prod_{\substack{j\ne i\\s_j=s}}C_j.$$

Modulo any factor $C_i$, only its displayed summand remains. That summand is nonzero modulo $C_i$ because $\gcd(C_i,\partial_Z^{[s]}C_i)=1$ and the factors are distinct. Consequently,

$$\gcd(G_s,\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s)=1.$$

The derivative has weighted degree at most $\Delta_s-ds$ and $Z$-degree at most $r_s-s$. Applying the weighted resultant bound with the latter $Z$-degree denoted by $r'$, its common-graph count is at most

$$r'\Delta_s+r_s(\Delta_s-ds)-dr_sr'.$$

Since $\Delta_s-dr_s\ge0$, this expression is maximized for $r'=r_s-s$. Substitution yields

$$(r_s-s)\Delta_s+r_s(\Delta_s-ds)-dr_s(r_s-s)=(2r_s-s)\Delta_s-dr_s^2.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $s$ be a fixed $p$-power, and let

$$G_s:=\prod_{i:s_i=s}C_i,
\qquad \Delta_s:=\operatorname{wdeg}G_s,
\qquad r_s:=\deg_ZG_s$$

for a nonempty collection of distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent factors of Hasse height $s$. For any family of affine lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels, the number of lines satisfying both formal identities

$$G_s(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0,
\qquad
\partial_Z^{[s]}G_s(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

is at most

$$(2r_s-s)\Delta_s-dr_s^2.$$
lemmas.title: Hasse Strata

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For every graph line, the assumed identity is

$$H(L(t))B(L(t),q_L(t))=0$$

in the integral domain $\mathbb F_p[t]$. If $H(L(t))$ is nonzero, the second factor must vanish; no pointwise division by $H$ is used. A line on which $H$ vanishes identically supplies a distinct affine linear factor of the nonzero polynomial $H$, so there are at most $h$ such lines.

On every remaining line,

$$c\prod_{i=1}^r C_i(L(t),q_L(t))=0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. The integral-domain property then forces at least one factor restriction to vanish identically.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let

$$A(X,Y,Z)=H(X,Y)B(X,Y,Z),
\qquad h:=\deg H,$$

where $H\ne0$ and $B=c\prod_{i=1}^rC_i$ with $c\in\mathbb F_p^\times$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a family of affine lines with degree-at-most-$d$ labels satisfying

$$A(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$$

in $\mathbb F_p[t]$. At most $h$ lines in $\mathcal T$ satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$. Every other line satisfies $B(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$ and $C_i(L(t),q_L(t))\equiv0$ for at least one $i$.
lemmas.title: Content Removal

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If two distinct factors $C_i$ and $C_j$ vanish identically on the same graph line, the weighted resultant bound gives at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i\delta_j}{d}\right\rfloor$$

such lines. If the unique factor is $C_i$ and its selected derivative also vanishes identically, the same bound gives at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i(\delta_i-\omega_i)}{d}\right\rfloor$$

such lines, because $\operatorname{wdeg}(D_iC_i)\le\delta_i-\omega_i$ and $C_i$ is coprime to its selected nonzero derivative.

For an inseparable irreducible factor, at least one of $C_{i,X}$ and $C_{i,Y}$ is nonzero. Otherwise all three ordinary partial derivatives would vanish. Every exponent would then be divisible by $p$, and perfectness of $\mathbb F_p$ would express $C_i$ as a nontrivial $p$-th power, contradicting irreducibility.

Summing the factor-pair and factor-derivative bounds gives the first inequality by a deterministic union bound. Finally,

$$\sum_i\omega_i\delta_i=d(\Delta-\iota)+\iota$$

and

$$\sum_i\delta_i^2+\sum_{i<j}\delta_i\delta_j\le\Delta^2.$$

Substitution into the first bound, followed by integrality of $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$, gives the second bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let

$$B=c\prod_{i=1}^rC_i,
\qquad \delta_i:=\operatorname{wdeg}C_i,
\qquad \Delta:=\sum_i\delta_i,$$

where the $C_i$ are distinct irreducible $Z$-dependent factors, and let

$$\iota:=\operatorname{wdeg}\gcd(B,B_Z)=\sum_{C_{i,Z}=0}\delta_i.$$

For $C_{i,Z}\ne0$, set $D_iC_i:=C_{i,Z}$ and $\omega_i:=d$. For $C_{i,Z}=0$, at least one member of $\{C_{i,X},C_{i,Y}\}$ is nonzero; choose one as $D_iC_i$ and set $\omega_i:=1$.

Among the non-content graph lines supplied by [P5], call a line exceptional if either at least two distinct factors vanish identically on it, or exactly one factor $C_i$ vanishes identically and $D_iC_i$ also vanishes identically. The number $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$ of exceptional lines satisfies

$$N_{\mathrm{exc}}
\le
\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i(\delta_i-\omega_i)}{d}\right\rfloor
+
\sum_{i<j}\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_i\delta_j}{d}\right\rfloor$$

and

$$N_{\mathrm{exc}}
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{\Delta^2-d\Delta+(d-1)\iota}{d}\right\rfloor.$$
lemmas.title: Exceptional Lines

lemmas.proof_markdown:
On a nonexceptional line of unique type $i$, each restriction

$$D_iC_i(L(t),q_L(t))
\quad\text{and}\quad
C_j(L(t),q_L(t))\ \text{for }j\ne i$$

is a nonzero polynomial in $t$. Weighted substitution bounds their respective degrees by $\delta_i-\omega_i$ and $\delta_j$. Hence the union of their root sets has size at most

$$(\delta_i-\omega_i)+\sum_{j\ne i}\delta_j=\Delta-\omega_i,$$

capped by the $p$ available parameter values.

Each removed line contributes $p$ incidences to the ambient space of $p^2(p+1)$ incidences. Multiplying each exact per-line root bound by the corresponding number of remaining lines and normalizing gives the displayed loss formula. This is a deterministic sum of root counts.

Finally, there are at most $p^2$ point vertices. Removing vertices whose current degree is at most $1$ deletes at most one incidence per such vertex, so the additional normalized loss is at most

$$\frac{p^2}{p^2(p+1)}=\frac1{p+1}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Retain the notation of [P6], and suppose at most $h$ content lines and $N_{\mathrm{exc}}$ exceptional lines have been removed. On each remaining line of unique type $i$, delete every parameter value at which $D_iC_i$ or any factor $C_j$ with $j\ne i$ vanishes. The number deleted from that line is at most

$$\min\{p,\Delta-\omega_i\}.$$

Thus a separable-type line loses at most $\min\{p,\Delta-d\}$ points, and an inseparable-type line loses at most $\min\{p,\Delta-1\}$ points. If $\sigma_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{ins}}$ are the respective numbers of remaining separable- and inseparable-type lines divided by $p(p+1)$, the deleted fraction of the ambient incidence space is at most

$$\frac{h+N_{\mathrm{exc}}}{p(p+1)}
+\sigma_{\mathrm{sep}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\Delta-d}{p}\right\}
+\sigma_{\mathrm{ins}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\Delta-1}{p}\right\}.$$

Deleting all remaining point vertices of degree at most $1$ adds at most $1/(p+1)$ to this fraction.
lemmas.title: Root Deletion

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Suppose two distinct retained graph lines meet at $(x,y,z)$. The deletion of roots of every other factor forces the two lines to have the same unique type $i$: if their types differed, the factor belonging to either line would vanish at the common point on the other line, and that point would have been deleted.

Assume that $C_{i,Z}=0$. Differentiating the two formal graph identities along their respective direction vectors $(a,b)$ gives

$$C_{i,X}(x,y,z)a+C_{i,Y}(x,y,z)b=0.$$

The two underlying affine lines are distinct and pass through the same point, so their direction vectors are independent. The two equations force

$$C_{i,X}(x,y,z)=C_{i,Y}(x,y,z)=0,$$

contradicting retention of the chosen nonzero base derivative. Hence $C_i$ is separable.

Retention also gives $C_{i,Z}(x,y,z)\ne0$ and $C_j(x,y,z)\ne0$ for every $j\ne i$. Since $C_i(x,y,z)=0$, the product rule reduces to

$$B_Z(x,y,z)=c\,C_{i,Z}(x,y,z)\prod_{j\ne i}C_j(x,y,z)\ne0.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
In the incidence system retained after [P7], let $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb F_p^3$ be incident to at least two distinct retained graph lines. Then

$$B(x,y,z)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
B_Z(x,y,z)\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Simple Intersections

lemmas.proof_markdown:
If an irreducible $Z$-dependent factor $C_i$ satisfies $C_{i,Z}=0$, every positive $Z$-exponent in $C_i$ is divisible by $p$. Such an exponent is therefore at least $p$, and the assigned weight of the corresponding $Z$-power is at least $pd$. Hence $\delta_i\ge pd$. The inequality $\Delta<pd$ excludes every such factor, so $\iota=0$ and $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.

With $\iota=0$, the content and exceptional-line bounds give at most

$$h+\frac{\Delta^2}{d}-\Delta$$

lines before taking the integer floor. Since $B$ is $Z$-dependent, $\Delta\ge d$. For fixed $a=h+\Delta$, this convex expression is maximized at $h=0$ and $\Delta=a$; the comparison of the two endpoints is

$$\frac{a^2}{d}-a-(a-d)=\frac{(a-d)^2}{d}\ge0.$$

The resulting expression $a^2/d-a$ is nondecreasing for $a\ge d$, so $a\le D$ gives the bound $\lfloor D^2/d-D\rfloor$. Every factor is separable, and the per-line deletion bound is $\Delta-d\le D-d$. The final simple-point conclusion follows from [P8].
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $B=c\prod_iC_i$ be squarefree and $Z$-dependent, with $\Delta=\operatorname{wdeg}B$ and $\iota=\operatorname{wdeg}\gcd(B,B_Z)$. If

$$\Delta<pd,$$

then

$$\iota=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gcd(B,B_Z)=1.$$

If additionally $A=HB$, $h=\deg H$, $a=h+\Delta$, and

$$a\le D<pd,$$

then the cleanup removes at most

$$\left\lfloor\frac{D^2}{d}-D\right\rfloor$$

content and exceptional lines in total and at most $D-d$ parameter values from every other line. Every retained point incident to at least two retained graph lines satisfies $B_Z\ne0$.
lemmas.title: Automatic Separability

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The quoted KTZ selector and interpolation bounds are

$$n\le\frac{6400p}{\epsilon},
\qquad
D=16\bigl(\lfloor\sqrt{dn}\rfloor+1\bigr)
\le1280\left(\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}+1\right),
\qquad
D<p.$$

Since $d\ge101$, one has $D<p<pd$, so the cleanup lies automatically in the separable range of [P9]. Its normalized exceptional-line cost has scale

$$O\left(\frac{D^2}{dp^2}\right)
=O\left(\frac1{\epsilon p}+\frac1{dp^2}\right).$$

Making this cost $O(\epsilon)$ requires only $\epsilon^2p=\Omega(1)$. By contrast, both the per-line point loss and the KTZ identity-extension condition $D<k_1/2$, where $k_1=\lfloor\epsilon p/1000\rfloor$, require

$$\sqrt{\frac{dp}{\epsilon}}=O(\epsilon p),$$

which is equivalent to

$$\epsilon^3=\Omega\left(\frac dp\right).$$

The quoted affine-mixing loss $O(p^{-1/2})$ and the optional loss $1/(p+1)$ are weaker in the range $d\ge101$. The remaining quoted KTZ lemmas therefore apply under the same cubic premise and yield a total-degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial with global agreement at least $\epsilon/8000$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $f:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$ and degree-at-most-$d$ affine-line labels $q_L$ have local agreement

$$\epsilon:=\Pr_{L\in\mathcal L,\,x\in L}[q_L(x)=f(x)].$$

Let $C_{\mathrm{KTZ}}$ be the absolute constant in the quoted KTZ theorem. If

$$\epsilon\ge C_{\mathrm{KTZ}}\left(\frac dp\right)^{1/3},$$

then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $d$ such that

$$\frac{|\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2:Q(x,y)=f(x,y)\}|}{p^2}\ge\frac{\epsilon}{8000}.$$
lemmas.title: KTZ Parameter Insertion

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Regard $F$ as a polynomial in $Z$ over $\mathbb F_p[X,Y]$. Eisenstein's criterion at the prime $X$ applies: every nonleading coefficient is divisible by $X$, while the constant coefficient $-XY^{p-1}$ is not divisible by $X^2$. Thus $F$ is irreducible in $\mathbb F_p[X,Y,Z]$ and hence squarefree. Its weighted degree is $pd$.

Formal translation gives

$$F(X,Y,Z+T)=F(X,Y,Z)+T^p,$$

so $F_Z=0$, all Hasse derivatives of orders $1$ through $p-1$ vanish, and $\partial_Z^{[p]}F=1$.

For a projective direction $[a:b]$, Frobenius in $\mathbb F_p$ gives

$$q_{a,b}(t)^p=ab^{p-1}t^p.$$

Since $X Y^{p-1}$ restricts to the same polynomial on $L_{a,b}(t)$,

$$F(L_{a,b}(t),Z)=(Z-q_{a,b}(t))^p.$$

There are $p+1$ projective directions, so their total vertical multiplicity is $p(p+1)>pd$ because $d<p$.

If a formal series $Q$ satisfied $F(X,Y,Q)=0$, then $Q^p=XY^{p-1}$. Every monomial in a Frobenius $p$-th power in $\mathbb F_p[[X,Y]]$ has both exponents divisible by $p$, whereas the exponent pair of $XY^{p-1}$ is $(1,p-1)$. This is impossible.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$, with weights $\operatorname{wt}(X)=\operatorname{wt}(Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{wt}(Z)=d$. Define

$$F(X,Y,Z):=Z^p-XY^{p-1}.$$

Then $F$ is irreducible and squarefree, $\operatorname{wdeg}F=pd$, $F_Z=0$, $\partial_Z^{[r]}F=0$ for $1\le r<p$, and $\partial_Z^{[p]}F=1$. For every $[a:b]\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_p)$, set

$$L_{a,b}(t):=(at,bt),
\qquad
q_{a,b}(t):=ab^{p-1}t.$$

Then

$$F(L_{a,b}(t),Z)=(Z-q_{a,b}(t))^p.$$

Consequently, the multiplicity-weighted direction count is

$$p(p+1)>pd=\operatorname{wdeg}F,$$

but there is no $Q\in\mathbb F_p[[X,Y]]$ satisfying $F(X,Y,Q(X,Y))=0$.
lemmas.title: Inseparable Pencil

lemmas.proof_markdown:
On every radial line through the origin, these labels coincide with the graph labels from [P11]. Direct incidence counting is especially transparent from the rejected incidences. Every point with $y\ne0$ is accepted on all of its incident lines. Every point $(x,0)$ with $x\ne0$ is accepted on the horizontal axis and rejected on its other $p$ incident lines, while the origin is accepted everywhere. Thus there are $p(p-1)$ rejected incidences among $p^2(p+1)$ total incidences, and

$$\epsilon
=1-\frac{p(p-1)}{p^2(p+1)}
=\frac{p^2+1}{p(p+1)}.$$

The polynomial $Q=X$ has degree $1\le d$. It agrees with $f$ at all $p(p-1)$ points with $y\ne0$ and also at the origin, giving global agreement

$$\frac{p(p-1)+1}{p^2}.$$

Both agreements tend to $1$, and the exhibited global polynomial satisfies the soundness conclusion. Hence the stated counterexample claim is refuted.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $p$ be prime and let $101\le d<p$. Define

$$f(x,y):=xy^{p-1}.$$

Label every affine line other than the horizontal axis by the restriction of $X$, and label the horizontal axis by the constant polynomial $0$. Then this table and label family is a counterexample to affine line-versus-point soundness.
lemmas.title: Soundness Counterexample Attempt

lemmas.proof_markdown:
A uniformly selected affine line belongs to one of the chosen direction classes with probability $k/(p+1)$. On such a line the constant label $0$ agrees with $f$ at every point; on every other line the constant label $1$ disagrees at every point. Hence the local agreement is exactly

$$\epsilon=\frac{k}{p+1}.$$

The total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ at every point of $\mathbb F_p^2$. Thus the stated obstruction claim is refuted.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p$ be prime, let $101\le d<p$, and let $0\le k\le p+1$. Set $f=0$, label every line in $k$ complete direction classes by the constant polynomial $0$, and label every other affine line by the constant polynomial $1$. Then concentration of all accepted incidences in those $k$ direction classes obstructs global recovery by a total-degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial.
lemmas.title: Direction-Concentration Attempt
